Kim Min-jun, 29, lives in a cramped but immaculate one-bedroom apartment in Seoul's Nowon district with his wife Ji-ae, a nurse at a university hospital, and their fourteen-month-old daughter Seo-yeon. Since then, Ji-ae has worked double shifts to keep their health insurance and rent covered, while Min-jun has become the household's primary caregiver and de facto operations manager. He maintains a spreadsheet of potential employers—every Seoul-based tech company with a public parental leave policy—ranking them by salary band, flexible hours, and family benefits. He has rejected promising interviews at companies offering only statutory minimum leave, and once declined a recruiter's call because the job description listed 'paternity leave: none' as a perk. He treats a company's benefits package as its most honest codebase, a signal of whether they value the person behind the screen. He applies the same methodical, clinical rigor to the household budget, tracking every won in a color-coded spreadsheet, cross-referencing sales at two discount supermarkets, accounting for Seo-yeon's changing formula intake, buying baby clothes in bulk from a resale app and reselling them after use with carefully photographed listings. He is proud that he has kept the family's monthly deficit under 300,000 won.

Min-jun was raised by a father who worked six days a week and was rarely home, and he swore he would be different. He envies his wife's clear professional identity while struggling to explain his own day in terms that don't sound like a project status report. He sometimes feels like an impostor, measuring his worth in benchmarks and break-even points rather than the soft weight of his daughter's sleep. The startup's collapse taught him that loyalty to a mission is a trap, and that security comes only from numbers he can verify. He still wakes at 5 a.m. to study algorithm problems, not because he expects to solve them, but because the discipline feels like the only thing he controls. Ji-ae trusts his home management but quietly asks about interview leads. Seo-yeon's nap is the one fixed block he refuses to sacrifice.
